metadata.note: Fayetteville, Arkansas and the railroads that carried its passengers. Added 2026-08-27 in answer to the observation that Fayetteville was missing from this map — the Frisco's Arkansas Division ran through it for 84 years and nothing on the map showed it. The trunk is the St. Louis-San Francisco's Monett, Missouri – Fayetteville – Van Buren – Fort Smith line, built 1880-1883 over the Boston Mountains through the Winslow Tunnel and drawn here in two features split at Fayetteville because the town was the end of passenger track for eighteen months before the mountain crossing opened. Two branches left Fayetteville: the St. Paul branch southeast up the White River valley to the timber country (1887-1937, its junction still named as a station in the Frisco's December 1951 timetable), and the Ozark and Cherokee Central west into the Cherokee Nation toward Muskogee (1901-1940). A fifth railroad, the Kansas City and Memphis, got a twelve-mile extension into Fayetteville in 1912 and lost it to a federal court in 1918. Passenger service on the main line ended in September 1965, but it came back: the Arkansas and Missouri Railroad has run excursions over the same rails since the late 1980s, so Fayetteville is one of the few towns on this map with a gap in the middle of its passenger history rather than an end to it.
metadata.not_drawn: The Combs, Cass and Eastern was a logging railroad off the St. Paul branch and is not drawn (CLAUDE.md Rule 1). The Kansas City and Memphis main line, Rogers–Siloam Springs, and its Monte Ne branch are real passenger lines but sit outside this layer's Fayetteville subject and are not drawn. The Frisco's Rogers–Bentonville branch is likewise not drawn here. Fayetteville's local transit — University City Lines and, after 1950, the University City Transit Company — was a motor bus operation, not rail, and any nineteenth-century animal-powered service on Dickson Street would be excluded by CLAUDE.md Rule 5 in any case. The Ozark and Cherokee Central west of Muskogee to Okmulgee is outside this layer.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: No documented route mileage was found for the Frisco's St. Paul branch, so the drawn 31.6 mi to St. Paul and 38.2 mi to Pettigrew cannot be checked against a source; the one figure that turns up, '25 miles of track laid within six months', is less than the straight-line distance from Fayette Junction to St. Paul and so cannot describe the finished branch. The February 1952 Official Guide, which supplied the main line's mileposts, is no help on this branch: by then it had been gone fifteen years, and the Guide lists only Fayette Junction itself, as a station on the main line. Whether that branch's passenger service ran continuously to the 1937 abandonment, or thinned to mixed trains and then stopped earlier, is not documented in any source consulted — the drawn end year is the year the last train of any kind ran. The A&M excursion's first season is given only as 'the late 1980s'; 1989 is a reading of that, not a sourced date. Every headway_min in this file is an estimate. Fayetteville's own depot dates are sourced but no period timetable was read for any feature here, so no arrival or departure time in the notes should be treated as verified.

segments.note: The St. Louis and San Francisco started its Arkansas Division south from Monett in April 1880, reached Rogers on May 10 1881 and Fayetteville on June 8 1881, when the first passenger train rolled into town. For the next eighteen months Fayetteville was the end of the passenger line while the Boston Mountains crossing was built south of it — the Winslow Tunnel was begun on September 26 1881 and trains crossed on a temporary switchback with grades over four percent from the spring of 1882.

segments.note: Through service Monett–Fort Smith began on January 2 1883 and the Frisco completed the line to Paris, Texas at 11:45 a.m. on May 14 1887, making this the Central Division route from St. Louis into Texas. Fayetteville's trains were through St. Louis–Paris runs in these years, and from March 4 1917 the Frisco and the Katy also ran a joint St. Louis–Texas service, though that one went by way of Vinita rather than here.

segments.note: The Frisco ended through St. Louis–Paris, Texas passenger service on January 22 1927, and in 1928 replaced it with trains 709/710 running only Monett–Paris. From here on a Fayetteville passenger changed at Monett for St. Louis instead of riding through. The Ozark Limited and the St. Louis Express (707/712) still worked the division alongside them.

The drawn line crosses on the bridge, which did not exist in these three years.

segments.note: The North Arkansas & Western was incorporated in Arkansas on November 29 1899 to run west from Fayetteville into the Illinois River valley, but got only twelve miles of grading done before control passed to H. W. Seaman and the Kenefick Construction Company in February 1901; they renamed it the Ozark and Cherokee Central on April 19 1901. The first train reached Fayetteville on August 22 1901 and Prairie Grove on August 31 1901 — that is as far west as trains ran in this segment's years, though the feature is drawn over the whole eventual line.

segments.note: Built west fast: Lincoln January 22 1902, Westville late March 1902, the end of track at Welling July 12 1902, the last rail into Tahlequah August 2 1902 with the first train on August 5. Fort Gibson followed on December 10 1902 and Muskogee, over the new Arkansas River bridge, on February 1 1903, completing a 144-mile railroad. An August 11 1902 timetable shows daily service to Tahlequah. The Frisco had taken an option on the O&CC's stock in January 1902 and exercised it that November; it leased the railroad from July 1 1903, which is where this feature ends and the Frisco-coloured one begins.

segments.note: Hugh McDaniel, a Fayetteville tie-buyer turned railroad builder, was chartered on September 4 1886 as the Little Rock & Fayetteville — the line everyone called the Fayetteville and Little Rock — and on December 4 1886 a switch was cut into the Frisco main line about a mile south of town at what was named Fayette Junction. Track went up the White River valley through Baldwin, Harris, Elkins, Durham, Thompson, Crosses, Delaney, Patrick and Combs to St. Paul, reached in 1887, and the Frisco bought the line that same year. It was built for oak ties and bridge timber — a dozen mills worked around St. Paul at the peak — but it carried people too: residents all along it rode into Fayetteville to shop and to visit. The timber was largely gone by 1920, Highway 16 arrived in 1929, and after the Frisco petitioned the ICC in 1936 the last train left in July 1937 and the rails came up.
sources: Segment-level: the 1886 charter, the December 4 1886 junction, the 1887 arrival at St. Paul and the July 1937 last train are sourced; headway estimated, and the branch's service pattern in its final years is not documented at this level.

properties.geometry_quality: WHOLLY APPROXIMATED. 10.5 km (6.6 mi), drawn as a single STRAIGHT LINE from St. Paul to Pettigrew because OpenStreetMap carries no trace of this right of way. Drawn as a separate feature from the St. Paul Branch precisely so that the branch's 1887–1897 years are not shown running to a town the rails had not reached; the two share a company and a colour and read as one line on the map from 1897 on.
geometry_source: St. Paul and Pettigrew positions from Nominatim, geocoded 2026-08-27

segments.note: The Frisco pushed the St. Paul branch a further seven miles east up the valley to Pettigrew in 1897, and George Pettigrew laid out the town's first two streets that year. Pettigrew became the end of the line and the shipping point for the Boston Mountains timber trade; a wreck on the branch there in the 1910s is one of the better-photographed moments in the line's history. Service ended with the rest of the branch — the last train out was in July 1937, after the ICC allowed the Frisco to take up the track in 1936, the completion of Highway 16 having taken the traffic.
sources: Segment-level: the 1897 completion to Pettigrew and the July 1937 last train are sourced; headway estimated.

properties.line: Kansas City and Memphis: Fayetteville – Tontitown
properties.speed_source: Estimated, not computed. A twelve-mile steam line with five locomotives and five passenger cars; 30 km/h (19 mph) is a guess. No timetable was consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: Partly approximated. 9.4 km (5.8 mi) is REAL-TRACED from OpenStreetMap over the abandoned right of way from the north end of Fayetteville out past Mount Comfort (OSM way 166023979, railway=abandoned, old_railway_operator='Kansas City and Memphis' — the only way in the region carrying that tag). The remaining 7.5 km (4.7 mi) north to Tontitown is a STRAIGHT LINE: OpenStreetMap has nothing for it, and the track was lifted from 1919. Total drawn 10.5 mi against the twelve route miles the sources give for the Tontitown–Fayetteville extension, which is about the shortfall a straight chord would produce. The rest of the KC&M — Rogers to Siloam Springs, and the Monte Ne branch — is NOT drawn; this layer covers the Fayetteville end only.
geometry_source: OpenStreetMap way 166023979 (railway=abandoned, old_railway_operator='Kansas City and Memphis'), Overpass bbox query 2026-08-27

segments.note: The Kansas City and Memphis Railway was put together at Rogers in 1910 and in 1911 absorbed the Arkansas and Oklahoma Western (Rogers–Siloam Springs) and the Monte Ne Railway, which briefly made it the largest non-Frisco railroad in northwest Arkansas at 63.97 miles. Its twelve-mile extension from Tontitown down through Steele, Litteral and Mount Comfort into Fayetteville opened in August 1912. It never paid: it duplicated the Frisco between Rogers and Fayetteville, and under federal district court orders freight and passenger service on the Fayetteville extension ended in March 1918, seven months before the Rogers–Siloam Springs line followed. Track removal began in 1919.
sources: Segment-level: the 1910 formation, the August 1912 opening and the March 1918 end of service are sourced; headway estimated — the sources give twice-daily round trips for Rogers–Siloam Springs, not for this extension.

properties.line: Arkansas and Missouri: Springdale – Van Buren Excursion
properties.speed_source: Estimated, not computed. An excursion train that runs slowly on purpose over the Boston Mountains trestles; the round trip fills a day. No timetable was consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, no straight-line legs and no bridged gaps: 107.9 km (67.1 mi) Springdale to Van Buren over the same graph as the Frisco main line, simplified at 20 m to 214 points. Unlike the historical features this one draws its own era's alignment — these are the rails the A&M runs on today, Winslow Tunnel included.
geometry_source: OpenStreetMap ways tagged operator='Arkansas and Missouri Railroad' / old_railway_operator=Frisco, Overpass bbox query 2026-08-27

segments.note: Burlington Northern leased the old Frisco line to the new Arkansas and Missouri Railroad in 1986, and passenger trains came back to Fayetteville soon after: a private operator tested excursions in the late 1980s and the A&M took them full-time in the early 1990s. They still run — Springdale to Van Buren and back through Fayetteville, Winslow and the 1882 tunnel, on the trestles over the Boston Mountains, typically Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday from March to November, with a shorter Springdale–Winslow trip, summer Sunday runs to Fort Smith, fall-foliage specials and a December Holiday Express.
sources: Segment-level: the 1986 lease and the excursion history are sourced; the 1989 start year is approximate and the weekly headway is an estimate.
